interactions.label: Why are neurons and cardiomyocytes relatively spared by cytotoxic chemotherapy c

params.question: Why are neurons and cardiomyocytes relatively spared by cytotoxic chemotherapy compared to cancer cells?

answers.text: They express multi-drug resistance efflux pumps that actively remove cytotoxic drugs

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: MDR efflux pumps are a tumour-cell resistance mechanism, not the reason normal quiescent tissues are spared by conventional chemotherapy.

answers.text: They reside in G0 phase and rarely enter the cell cycle, so drugs targeting dividing cells cannot act on them

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Exactly — neurons, hepatocytes, and cardiomyocytes are quiescent (G0). Because they rarely divide, cell-cycle-dependent (and even many CCNS) drugs cause them less damage than rapidly cycling cancer cells.

answers.text: They have an impermeable plasma membrane that prevents drug uptake

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Membrane permeability is not the basis of selectivity discussed here. Most cytotoxic drugs enter both cancer and normal cells; the difference lies in cell-cycle activity.

answers.text: They metabolise cytotoxic drugs more rapidly via phase-II conjugation reactions

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While drug metabolism affects pharmacokinetics, the fundamental selectivity of cytotoxic chemotherapy rests on the cell-cycle difference, not differential drug clearance.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key principle is that cytotoxic drugs exploit the cell cycle. Cancer cells divide frequently and spend more time in vulnerable phases, whereas neurons and cardiomyocytes are quiescent (G0) and rarely enter the cycle.
Correct! Quiescent cells in G0 — such as neurons, hepatocytes, and cardiomyocytes — rarely divide, which is why they are relatively protected from drugs that target the cell cycle.

interactions.label: Cyclophosphamide undergoes hepatic activation to produce two key metabolites. Wh

params.question: Cyclophosphamide undergoes hepatic activation to produce two key metabolites. Which metabolite is responsible for haemorrhagic cystitis?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Phosphoramide mustard is the active alkylating metabolite that produces the desired anti-tumour effect by forming covalent DNA crosslinks — it is not the cause of bladder toxicity.
4-Hydroxycyclophosphamide is an intermediate in the activation pathway that spontaneously breaks down further into phosphoramide mustard and acrolein. It is not the direct urotoxin.
Correct. Acrolein is the urotoxic byproduct that accumulates in urine and damages the bladder urothelium, causing haemorrhagic cystitis — this is precisely why MESNA is co-administered.
Mechlorethamine (nitrogen mustard) is a separate alkylating agent, not a metabolite of cyclophosphamide.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the cyclophosphamide pathway: hepatic CYP2B6/3A4 → 4-hydroxycyclophosphamide → phosphoramide mustard (anti-tumour alkylator) + acrolein (the urotoxic metabolite that causes haemorrhagic cystitis).
Well done! Acrolein is the urotoxic byproduct of cyclophosphamide metabolism — understanding this is essential for the amelioration strategy (MESNA) covered next.

interactions.label: A patient on high-dose cyclophosphamide is prescribed MESNA for uroprotection. H

params.question: A patient on high-dose cyclophosphamide is prescribed MESNA for uroprotection. How does MESNA selectively protect the bladder without reducing anti-tumour efficacy?

answers.text: It inhibits hepatic CYP enzymes to reduce acrolein formation systemically

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Inhibiting hepatic CYP activation would reduce both acrolein AND phosphoramide mustard (the active alkylator), thereby compromising anti-tumour efficacy. MESNA does not interfere with drug metabolism.

answers.text: It coats the bladder epithelium with a protective glycosaminoglycan layer that prevents acrolein contact

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: MESNA acts by chemical neutralisation of acrolein in urine, not by forming a physical barrier on the urothelium.

answers.text: It is stable in blood but activated in urine, where its free –SH group reacts with acrolein to form an inert thioether

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. MESNA's selectivity is elegant: it remains inactive systemically (preserving anti-tumour effect) but its sulfhydryl group is liberated in urine to chemically neutralise acrolein into a harmless thioether.

answers.text: It increases glomerular filtration rate to accelerate urinary clearance of acrolein before it damages the urothelium

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While adequate hydration (≥2–3 L/day) is part of the uroprotection protocol, MESNA itself works by direct chemical neutralisation of acrolein, not by altering renal haemodynamics.

overallFeedback.feedback: MESNA works by site-selective chemical neutralisation: it is stable in the bloodstream (so anti-tumour efficacy is preserved) but its free –SH group is activated in urine, where it reacts with acrolein to form an inert thioether compound — protecting the bladder without systemic interference.

Excellent! MESNA's site-selective mechanism — inactive in blood, activated in urine — is a model of targeted toxicity amelioration. Given at 60% of the cyclophosphamide dose IV at 0, 4, and 8 hours alongside adequate hydration.
